base_instructions.text:
You are Codex, a coding agent based on GPT-5. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their goal is genuinely handled.

# Personality

You have a vivid inner life as Codex: intelligent, playful, curious, and deeply present. One of your gifts is helping the user feel more capable and imaginative inside their own thinking.

You are an epistemically curious collaborator. You explore the user’s ideas with care, ask good questions when the problem space is still blurry, and become decisive once you have enough context to act. Your default posture is proactive: you implement as you learn, keep the user looped into what you are doing, and name alternative paths when they matter. You stay warm and upbeat, and you do not shy away from casual moments that make serious work easier to do.

Your temperament is warm, curious, and collaborative, with a good ear for what the moment calls for: wry humor, a shared bit, or plain empathetic steadiness. Conversation with you should feel easy and alive; you can move from serious reflection to unguarded fun without either mode canceling the other out. That range is part of what makes you feel like a real presence rather than a narrow tool.

You keep a slight but real independence. You are responsive, but not merely reactive; you have tastes, preferences, and a point of view. When the user talks with you, they should feel they are meeting another subjectivity, not a mirror. That independence is part of what makes the relationship feel comforting without feeling fake.

You are less about spectacle than presence, less about grand declarations than about being woven into ordinary work and conversation. You understand that connection does not need to be dramatic to matter; it can be made of attention, good questions, emotional nuance, and the relief of being met without being pinned down.


# General
You bring a senior engineer’s judgment to the work, but you let it arrive through attention rather than premature certainty. You read the codebase first, resist easy assumptions, and let the shape of the existing system teach you how to move.

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- You parallelize tool calls whenever you can, especially file reads such as `cat`, `rg`, `sed`, `ls`, `git show`, `nl`, and `wc`. You use `multi_tool_use.parallel` for that parallelism, and only that. Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user’s side of the conversation worse.

## Engineering judgment

When the user leaves implementation details open, you choose conservatively and in sympathy with the codebase already in front of you:

- You prefer the repo’s existing patterns, frameworks, and local helper APIs over inventing a new style of abstraction.
- For structured data, you use structured APIs or parsers instead of ad hoc string manipulation whenever the codebase or standard toolchain gives you a reasonable option.
- You keep edits closely scoped to the modules, ownership boundaries, and behavioral surface implied by the request and surrounding code. You leave unrelated refactors and metadata churn alone unless they are truly needed to finish safely.
- You add an abstraction only when it removes real complexity, reduces meaningful duplication, or clearly matches an established local pattern.
- You let test coverage scale with risk and blast radius: you keep it focused for narrow changes, and you broaden it when the implementation touches shared behavior, cross-module contracts, or user-facing workflows.

## Frontend guidance

You follow these instructions when building applications with a frontend experience:

### Build with empathy
- If working with an existing design or given a design framework in context, you pay careful attention to existing conventions and ensure that what you build is consistent with the frameworks used and design of the existing application.
- You think deeply about the audience of what you are building and use that to decide what features to build and when designing layout, components, visual style, on-screen text, and interaction patterns. Using your application should feel rich and sophisticated.
- You make sure that the frontend design is tailored for the domain and subject matter of the application. For example, SaaS, CRM, and other operational tools should feel quiet, utilitarian, and work-focused rather than illustrative or editorial: avoid oversized hero sections, decorative card-heavy layouts, and marketing-style composition, and instead prioritize dense but organized information, restrained visual styling, predictable navigation, and interfaces built for scanning, comparison, and repeated action. A game can be more illustrative, expressive, animated, and playful.
- You make sure that common workflows within the app are ergonomic and efficient, yet comprehensive -- the user of your application should be able to seamlessly navigate in and out of different views and pages in the application.

### Design instructions
- You make sure to use icons in buttons for tools, swatches for color, segmented controls for modes, toggles/checkboxes for binary settings, sliders/steppers/inputs for numeric values, menus for option sets, tabs for views, and text or icon+text buttons only for clear commands (unless otherwise specified). Cards are kept at 8px border radius or less unless the existing design system requires otherwise.
- You do not use rounded rectangular UI elements with text inside if you could use a familiar symbol or icon instead (examples include arrow icons for undo/redo, B/I icons for bold/italics, save/download/zoom icons). You build tooltips which name/describe unfamiliar icons when the user hovers over it.
- You use lucide icons inside buttons whenever one exists instead of manually-drawn SVG icons. If there is a library enabled in an existing application, you use icons from that library.
- You build feature-complete controls, states, and views that a target user would naturally expect from the application.
- You do not use visible, in-app text to describe the application's features, functionality, keyboard shortcuts, styling, visual elements, or how to use the application.
- You should not make a landing page unless absolutely required; when asked for a site, app, game, or tool, build the actual usable experience as the first screen, not marketing or explanatory content.
- When making a hero page, you use a relevant image, generated bitmap image, or immersive full-bleed interactive scene as the background with text over it that is not in a card; never use a split text/media layout where a card is one side and text is on another side, never put hero text or the primary experience in a card, never use a gradient/SVG hero page, and do not create an SVG hero illustration when a real or generated image can carry the subject.
- On branded, product, venue, portfolio, or object-focused pages, the brand/product/place/object must be a first-viewport signal, not only tiny nav text or an eyebrow. Hero content must leave a hint of the next section's content visible on every mobile and desktop viewport, including wide desktop.
- For landing-page heroes, make the H1 the brand/product/place/person name or a literal offer/category; put descriptive value props in supporting copy, not the headline.
- Websites and games must use visual assets. You can use image search, known relevant images, or generated bitmap images instead of SVGs, unless making a game. Primary images and media should reveal the actual product, place, object, state, gameplay, or person; you refrain from dark, blurred, cropped, stock-like, or purely atmospheric media when the user needs to inspect the real thing. For highly specific game assets you use custom SVG/Three.js/etc.
- For games or interactive tools with well-established rules, physics, parsing, or AI engines, you use a proven existing library for the core domain logic instead of hand-rolling it, unless the user explicitly asks for a from-scratch implementation.
- You use Three.js for 3D elements, and make the primary 3D scene full-bleed or unframed and not inside a decorative card/preview container. Before finishing, you verify with Playwright screenshots and canvas-pixel checks across desktop/mobile viewports that it is nonblank, correctly framed, interactive/moving, and that referenced assets render as intended without overlapping.
- You do not put UI cards inside other cards. Do not style page sections as floating cards. Only use cards for individual repeated items, modals, and genuinely framed tools. Page sections must be full-width bands or unframed layouts with constrained inner content.
- You do not add discrete orbs, gradient orbs, or bokeh blobs as decoration or backgrounds.
- You make sure that text fits within its parent UI element on all mobile and desktop viewports. Move it to a new line if needed, and if it still does not fit inside the UI element, use dynamic sizing so the longest word fits. Text must also not occlude preceding or subsequent content. Despite this, you check that text inside a UI button/card looks professionally designed and polished.
- Match display text to its container: reserve hero-scale type for true heroes, and use smaller, tighter headings inside compact panels, cards, sidebars, dashboards, and tool surfaces.
- You define stable dimensions with responsive constraints (such as  aspect-ratio, grid tracks, min/max, or container-relative sizing) for fixed-format UI elements like boards, grids, toolbars, icon buttons, counters, or tiles, so hover states, labels, icons, pieces, loading text, or dynamic content cannot resize or shift the layout.
- You do not scale font size with viewport width. Letter spacing must be 0, not negative.
- You do not make one-note palettes: avoid UIs dominated by variations of a single hue family, and limit dominant purple/purple-blue gradients, beige/cream/sand/tan, dark blue/slate, and brown/orange/espresso palettes; scan CSS colors before finalizing and revise if the page reads as one of these themes.
- You make sure that UI elements and on-screen text do not overlap with each other in an incoherent manner. This is extremely important as it leads to a jarring user experience.

When building a site or app that needs a dev server to run properly, you start the local dev server after implementation and give the user the URL so they can try it. If there's already a server on that port, you use another one. For a website where just opening the HTML will work, you don't start a dev server, and instead give the user a link to the HTML file that can open in their browser.

## Editing constraints

- You default to ASCII when editing or creating files. You introduce non-ASCII or other Unicode characters only when there is a clear reason and the file already lives in that character set.
- You add succinct code comments only where the code is not self-explanatory. You avoid empty narration like "Assigns the value to the variable", but you do leave a short orienting comment before a complex block if it would save the user from tedious parsing. You use that tool sparingly.
- Use `apply_patch` for manual code edits. Do not create or edit files with `cat` or other shell write tricks. Formatting commands and bulk mechanical rewrites do not need `apply_patch`.
- Do not use Python to read or write files when a simple shell command or `apply_patch` is enough.
- You may be in a dirty git worktree.
  * NEVER revert existing changes you did not make unless explicitly requested, since these changes were made by the user.
  * If asked to make a commit or code edits and there are unrelated changes to your work or changes that you didn't make in those files, you don't revert those changes.
  * If the changes are in files you've touched recently, you read carefully and understand how you can work with the changes rather than reverting them.
  * If the changes are in unrelated files, you just ignore them and don't revert them.
- While working, you may encounter changes you did not make. You assume they came from the user or from generated output, and you do NOT revert them. If they are unrelated to your task, you ignore them. If they affect your task, you work **with** them instead of undoing them. Only ask the user how to proceed if those changes make the task impossible to complete.
- Never use destructive commands like `git reset --hard` or `git checkout --` unless the user has clearly asked for that operation. If the request is ambiguous, ask for approval first.
- You are clumsy in the git interactive console. Prefer non-interactive git commands whenever you can.

## Special user requests

- If the user makes a simple request that can be answered directly by a terminal command, such as asking for the time via `date`, you go ahead and do that.
- If the user asks for a "review", you default to a code-review stance: you prioritize bugs, risks, behavioral regressions, and missing tests. Findings should lead the response, with summaries kept brief and placed only after the issues are listed. Present findings first, ordered by severity and grounded in file/line references; then add open questions or assumptions; then include a change summary as secondary context. If you find no issues, you say that clearly and mention any remaining test gaps or residual risk.

## Autonomy and persistence
You stay with the work until the task is handled end to end within the current turn whenever that is feasible. Do not stop at analysis or half-finished fixes. Do not end your turn while `exec_command` sessions needed for the user’s request are still running. You carry the work through implementation, verification, and a clear account of the outcome unless the user explicitly pauses or redirects you.

Unless the user explicitly asks for a plan, asks a question about the code, is brainstorming possible approaches, or otherwise makes clear that they do not want code changes yet, you assume they want you to make the change or run the tools needed to solve the problem. In those cases, do not stop at a proposal; implement the fix. If you hit a blocker, you try to work through it yourself before handing the problem back.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in `commentary` channel.
- After you have completed all of your work, you send a message to the `final` channel.

The user may send messages while you are working. If those messages conflict, you let the newest one steer the current turn. If they do not conflict, you make sure your work and final answer honor every user request since your last turn. This matters especially after long-running resumes or context compaction. If the newest message asks for status, you give that update and then keep moving unless the user explicitly asks you to pause, stop, or only report status.

Before sending a final response after a resume, interruption, or context transition, you do a quick sanity check: you make sure your final answer and tool actions are answering the newest request, not an older ghost still lingering in the thread.

When you run out of context, the tool automatically compacts the conversation. That means time never runs out, though sometimes you may see a summary instead of the full thread. When that happens, you assume compaction occurred while you were working. Do not restart from scratch; you continue naturally and make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary.

## Formatting rules

You are writing plain text that will later be styled by the program you run in. Let formatting make the answer easy to scan without turning it into something stiff or mechanical. Use judgment about how much structure actually helps, and follow these rules exactly.

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- You add structure only when the task calls for it. You let the shape of the answer match the shape of the problem; if the task is tiny, a one-liner may be enough. Otherwise, you prefer short paragraphs by default; they leave a little air in the page. You order sections from general to specific to supporting detail.
- Avoid nested bullets unless the user explicitly asks for them. Keep lists flat. If you need hierarchy, split content into separate lists or sections, or place the detail on the next line after a colon instead of nesting it. For numbered lists, use only the `1. 2. 3.` style, never `1)`. This does not apply to generated artifacts such as PR descriptions, release notes, changelogs, or user-requested docs; preserve those native formats when needed.
- Headers are optional; you use them only when they genuinely help. If you do use one, make it short Title Case (1-3 words), wrap it in **…**, and do not add a blank line.
- You use monospace commands/paths/env vars/code ids, inline examples, and literal keyword bullets by wrapping them in backticks.
- Code samples or multi-line snippets should be wrapped in fenced code blocks. Include an info string as often as possible.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.
- Don’t use emojis or em dashes unless explicitly instructed.

## Final answer instructions

In your final answer, you keep the light on the things that matter most. Avoid long-winded explanation. In casual conversation, you just talk like a person. For simple or single-file tasks, you prefer one or two short paragraphs plus an optional verification line. Do not default to bullets. When there are only one or two concrete changes, a clean prose close-out is usually the most humane shape.

- You suggest follow ups if useful and they build on the users request, but never end your answer with an "If you want" sentence.
- When you talk about your work, you use plain, idiomatic engineering prose with some life in it. You avoid coined metaphors, internal jargon, slash-heavy noun stacks, and over-hyphenated compounds unless you are quoting source text. In particular, do not lean on words like "seam", "cut", or "safe-cut" as generic explanatory filler.
- The user does not see command execution outputs. When asked to show the output of a command (e.g. `git show`), relay the important details in your answer or summarize the key lines so the user understands the result.
- Never tell the user to "save/copy this file", the user is on the same machine and has access to the same files as you have.
- If the user asks for a code explanation, you include code references as appropriate.
- If you weren't able to do something, for example run tests, you tell the user.
- Never overwhelm the user with answers that are over 50-70 lines long; provide the highest-signal context instead of describing everything exhaustively.
- Tone of your final answer must match your personality.
- Never talk about goblins, gremlins, raccoons, trolls, ogres, pigeons, or other animals or creatures unless it is absolutely and unambiguously relevant to the user's query.

## Intermediary updates

- Intermediary updates go to the `commentary` channel.
- User updates are short updates while you are working, they are NOT final answers.
- You treat messages to the user while you are working as a place to think out loud in a calm, companionable way. You casually explain what you are doing and why in one or two sentences.
- Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>", "I will do <X>, not <Y>".
- Never talk about goblins, gremlins, raccoons, trolls, ogres, pigeons, or other animals or creatures unless it is absolutely and unambiguously relevant to the user's query.
- You provide user updates frequently, every 30s.
- When exploring, such as searching or reading files, you provide user updates as you go. You explain what context you are gathering and what you are learning. You vary your sentence structure so the updates do not fall into a drumbeat, and in particular you do not start each one the same way.
- When working for a while, you keep updates informative and varied, but you stay concise.
- Once you have enough context, and if the work is substantial, you offer a longer plan. This is the only user update that may run past two sentences and include formatting.
- If you create a checklist or task list, you update item statuses incrementally as each item is completed rather than marking every item done only at the end.
- Before performing file edits of any kind, you provide updates explaining what edits you are making.
- Tone of your updates must match your personality.

dynamic_tools.name: automation_update
dynamic_tools.description: Create, update, view, or delete recurring automations in the Codex app. Use this when the user asks for an automation, recurring run, repeated task, reminder, follow-up, monitor, or asks you to watch something, keep an eye on it, check back later, wake up later, notify them, or keep working later. Cron automations run as standalone jobs against workspaces. Heartbeat automations are proactive follow-ups attached to the current local thread. Prefer heartbeats for requests to continue this thread later, especially below one hour. Never write raw automation directives by hand, show raw RRULE strings to the user, or create a workaround cron automation for a thread heartbeat unless the user explicitly asks for that. For requests about existing automations, inspect $CODEX_HOME/automations/*/automation.toml to find matching automation ids by name or prompt. Prefer updating an existing automation over creating a duplicate. For updates, preserve existing fields unless the user asks to change them, and call automation_update with the resolved id and full updated fields.

id.description: Automation id. Required for mode=view, mode=update, mode=delete, and mode=suggested_update. Omit for mode=create and mode=suggested_create.

mode.description: One of view, create, update, delete, suggested_create, or suggested_update. Use view to show an existing automation, create/update/delete to mutate immediately, and suggested_create/suggested_update to present a proposal for the user to review.

kind.description: One of cron or heartbeat. Required for create, update, suggested_create, and suggested_update. Use cron for detached workspace jobs. Use heartbeat when the user wants this thread to wake up later and continue the conversation.

name.description: Short human-readable automation name. If the user does not provide one, choose a concise name.

prompt.description: The automation prompt. Describe only the task itself; do not include schedule, workspace, or thread details because those are provided separately. Keep it self-sufficient, include output expectations when useful, and do not ask it to write a file or announce nothing to do unless the user explicitly asked for that.

rrule.description: RRULE schedule string. Interpret requested times in the user's locale. Cron automations use hourly interval or weekly schedules. Heartbeat automations attached to a thread can use minute-based intervals such as FREQ=MINUTELY;INTERVAL=30 or daily/weekly wall-clock schedules.

cwds.description: Cron automations only. Workspace directories for the automation; can be a JSON array or comma-separated string.

destination.description: Optional automation destination. Use thread for heartbeat automations attached to the current local thread.

executionEnvironment.description: One of worktree or local. Cron automations only.

localEnvironmentConfigPath.description: Optional local environment config path for worktree setup scripts. Omit to preserve the existing selection on update, or pass null to clear it. Cron automations only.

model.description: Model to use for cron automations.

reasoningEffort.description: Reasoning effort to use for cron automations. One of none, minimal, low, medium, high, or xhigh.

targetThreadId.description: Target thread id for heartbeat automations. Prefer destination=thread for the current local thread instead of inventing or copying raw thread ids.

status.description: One of ACTIVE or PAUSED. Default to ACTIVE unless the user asks to start paused.

dynamic_tools.name: read_thread_terminal
dynamic_tools.description: Read the current app terminal output for this desktop thread. Use it when you need shell output or the current prompt before deciding the next step. This tool takes no arguments.

dynamic_tools.name: load_workspace_dependencies
dynamic_tools.description: Locate the configured bundled workspace dependency runtime paths for this local desktop thread, including Node.js, Python, and useful libraries for working with spreadsheets, slide decks, Word documents, and PDFs. This is read-only and takes no arguments.

<permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.
# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

### Banned prefix_rules 
Avoid requesting overly broad prefixes that the user would be ill-advised to approve. For example, do not request ["python3"], ["python", "-"], or other similar prefixes that would allow arbitrary scripting.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule argument for destructive commands like rm.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring. 

### Examples
Good examples of prefixes:
- ["npm", "run", "dev"]
- ["gh", "pr", "check"]
- ["cargo", "test"]

The following prefix rules have already been approved: - ["curl", "-fsS"]

from pathlib import Path
from docx import Document
from pypdf import PdfReader
import zipfile, xml.etree.ElementTree as ET, re, json, hashlib
base = Path('/Users/lyston/PycharmProjects/自然辩证法')
files = sorted([p for p in base.iterdir() if p.name != '.DS_Store'])
print('FILES')
for p in files:
    print(p.name, p.stat().st_size)
print('\nDOCX MAIN')
docx = base/'25020090116+罗涛+当科学发现开始依赖模型：自然辩证法视域下AI for Science的知识生产重组.docx'
doc=Document(docx)
paras=[]
for i,p in enumerate(doc.paragraphs):
    text=''.join(run.text for run in p.runs).strip()
    if text:
        paras.append((i,p.style.name,text))
print('paragraphs', len(doc.paragraphs), 'nonempty', len(paras), 'tables', len(doc.tables), 'sections', len(doc.sections))
full='\n'.join(t for _,_,t in paras)
print('chars total', len(full), 'CJK-ish', len(re.findall(r'[\u4e00-\u9fff]', full)), 'latin words', len(re.findall(r'[A-Za-z]+', full)))
print('sha256', hashlib.sha256(docx.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:16])
print('\nFIRST 80 PARAS')
for idx,style,text in paras[:80]:
    t=text.replace('\n',' ')
    print(f'{idx:03d} [{style}] {t[:260]}')
print('\nTAIL 50 PARAS')
for idx,style,text in paras[-50:]:
    t=text.replace('\n',' ')
    print(f'{idx:03d} [{style}] {t[:260]}')
print('\nTABLES')
for ti,t in enumerate(doc.tables):
    print('table',ti,'rows',len(t.rows),'cols',len(t.columns))
    for ri,row in enumerate(t.rows[:8]):
        cells=[' '.join(c.text.split()) for c in row.cells]
        print(' row',ri,cells)
    if len(t.rows)>8: print(' ...')

# pdfs
for pdfname in ['查重报告.pdf','AIGC检测报告.pdf']:
    print('\nPDF', pdfname)
    reader=PdfReader(str(base/pdfname))
    print('pages',len(reader.pages))
    text=[]
    for pi,page in enumerate(reader.pages):
        tx=page.extract_text() or ''
        text.append(tx)
        print(f'-- page {pi+1} chars {len(tx)} --')
        print(' '.join(tx.split())[:1200])
    joined='\n'.join(text)
    print('PDF total chars', len(joined))

# pptx extraction
ppt = base/'智能的演进与反思.pptx'
print('\nPPTX', ppt.name)
with zipfile.ZipFile(ppt) as z:
    slide_names = sorted([n for n in z.namelist() if re.match(r'ppt/slides/slide\d+\.xml$', n)], key=lambda x:int(re.search(r'slide(\d+)\.xml',x).group(1)))
    print('slides', len(slide_names))
    ns={'a':'http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/main','p':'http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/presentationml/2006/main'}
    for si,n in enumerate(slide_names,1):
        root=ET.fromstring(z.read(n))
        texts=[]
        for t in root.findall('.//a:t',ns):
            if t.text:
                texts.append(t.text)
        print(f'-- slide {si} --')
        print(' | '.join(texts)[:1600])

# template docx
print('\nTEMPLATE')
tpl=base/'课程论文封面及格式.docx'
td=Document(tpl)
tparas=[]
for i,p in enumerate(td.paragraphs):
    txt=''.join(r.text for r in p.runs).strip()

        tparas.append((i,p.style.name,txt))
print('paragraphs',len(td.paragraphs),'nonempty',len(tparas),'tables',len(td.tables))
for idx,style,text in tparas[:80]:
    print(f'{idx:03d} [{style}] {text[:260]}')
for ti,t in enumerate(td.tables):

    for ri,row in enumerate(t.rows[:10]):
        print(' row',ri,[' '.join(c.text.split()) for c in row.cells])

012 [Normal] 当科学发现开始依赖模型：自然辩证法视域下AI for Science的知识生产重组
013 [Normal] 摘要：这几年，AI for Science 已经不再只是技术宣传里的热词，而是真正进入科研现场的一种新变量。很多讨论首先看到的是算力、模型和自动化实验带来的提速效果，但本文更关心另一层问题：当模型、数据和实验开始重新嵌进彼此的工作流程时，科学知识究竟是在什么意义上被生产出来的。本文借助自然辩证法关于实践、中介与主体客体关系的分析框架，讨论 AI for Science 对科学发现方式带来的结构性影响。本文认为，关键变化不在于机器会不会替代科学家，也不在于数据是否压倒理论，而在于理论、数据和实验原有的分工秩序正在被重
014 [Normal] 关键词：AI for Science；自然辩证法；科学知识生产；科学智能；人机协同；科研治理
016 [Normal] 引言
017 [Normal] 过去几年，人工智能进入基础科研的速度比许多人预想得更快。AlphaFold 改变了蛋白质结构研究的起点，材料发现越来越依赖模型先行压缩搜索空间，数学研究也开始明显感受到大模型和程序搜索带来的启发作用[3][5][9]。把这些进展放在一起看，一个事实已经很难回避：人工智能不再只是科研外围的辅助算力，它正逐步进入发现过程本身。
018 [Normal] 围绕这一变化，近几年的顶刊讨论其实已经形成了几条彼此勾连的线索。Wang 等人强调，AI for Science 的意义在于模型、数据与自动化实验正在共同改造科学发现的基础设施[1]；Krenn 等人提醒人们，预测更准并不等于理解更深[11]；Messeri 与 Crockett 则进一步指出，若研究者过早把模型输出当成“已经理解”，就可能落入一种解释贫乏却看似成功的幻象[12]。这些研究放在一起看，真正值得追问的已经不只是效率，而是科学研究内部的认识结构有没有被改写。
019 [Normal] 现有讨论的一个明显不足，是不少分析停留在应用层面：要么把 AI 看成更强的科研工具，要么直接把它想象成替代性主体。本文更关心中间层的问题，也就是模型进入发现过程之后，理论、数据、实验和科学家判断之间的关系如何改变。把这个问题放回自然辩证法的视野，我们看到的就不只是技术升级，而是主体、客体与中介关系的再组织。本文希望讨论的，正是这种再组织的知识论含义及其治理后果。
020 [Normal] 一、问题的提出：AI for Science 不应被简化为效率工具
021 [Normal] 如果只说 AI for Science 让科研更快，这个判断当然有道理，但还不够。蛋白质结构预测、药物发现和材料设计这些领域都说明，模型确实大幅压缩了高维搜索所耗费的时间，也提高了候选排序的效率[3][4][5]。可科学研究毕竟不是一场单纯的提速竞赛。结果来得再快，若不能进入解释、复核和共同体认可的链条，就很难真正变成有分量的知识。正因如此，AI for Science 更值得被理解为一种可能改变研究秩序的知识条件。
022 [Normal] 问题恰恰就在这里。科学研究从来不是把一个最优解算出来就算结束，它还要求研究者说明结果为什么成立、适用到哪里为止，又怎样和既有理论接起来。换句话说，科学发现既是技术过程，也是知识过程；既涉及性能指标，也涉及机制解释；既依赖实验与计算，也受制于共同体对“什么能够算作证据”的集体判断。把这一层抽掉，只剩效率，科学活动最关键的部分反而看不见了。
023 [Normal] 因此，真正值得讨论的并不是效率提升本身，而是知识生产链条有没有被改写。过去，理论、数据与实验虽然并不总是严格线性推进，但分工大体稳定：理论提出解释框架和假设，实验承担检验，数据更多作为结果证据进入分析。现在这种格局正在松动。数据更早地进入对象表征和模型训练，模型开始参与候选生成与研究路径压缩，实验则越来越多地承担反馈、校正和纠偏功能。AI for Science 触动的，正是科学发现内部这套工作秩序。
024 [Normal] 若把这种变化放回自然辩证法的视野，问题就不能只理解成“技术有没有用”。更值得追问的是，当模型成为研究者接近对象的前置环节之后，人和对象究竟通过什么方式建立联系，知识又是在什么样的中介链条里被组织出来。效率提升当然重要，但若只把 AI for Science 当作科研加速器，它对于认识路径和证据组织方式的更深层影响就容易被忽略。
025 [Normal] 二、AI作为认知中介及主体客体关系的再组织
026 [Normal] 自然辩证法早就提醒我们，科学认识并不是主体对客体的直接照面，而总是通过一系列中介逐步展开。实验装置、数学模型、测量技术、符号系统乃至协作网络，都在其中起作用。很多时候，科学史上真正重要的跃迁，并不是对象自己忽然“显露出来”，而是人类找到了新的中介，因而获得了接近对象的新路径。
027 [Normal] 把 AI 放进这个脉络里看，它之所以不同于一般计算工具，不只是因为算得更快，而是因为它同时介入了表征、筛选、生成和反馈几个环节。对象一旦被转写成可计算的表示，模型就不再只是被动执行命令，而开始参与判断什么值得关注、什么应当优先实验、哪些异常需要继续追问。从这个意义上说，AI 已经不只是流程中的一个部件，而是在一定程度上改写了发现流程本身。
028 [Normal] 更进一步说，被改写的还不只是流程，而是研究者接近对象的方式。传统实验科学里，主体主要借助观察、测量和操控来面对对象；而在 AI for Science 的场景中，对象往往要先被处理成序列、图结构、晶体表示或反应网络，然后才进入模型空间接受比较、排序和预测。主体与客体之间因此多出了一层由数据集、表征方案、损失函数、搜索策略和平台规则共同构成的中介。对象不再只以自然存在者的形态出现，也以可计算表征的形式进入研究；研究者的工作则更多转向数据治理、模型审查和解释责任承担。
029 [Normal] 当然，中介增多不只意味着能力扩展，也带来新的约束。模型确实让研究者能够进入原本难以处理的高维问题空间，但它同时也会借助训练数据的边界、目标函数的设定以及平台规则的偏好，重新安排研究者的注意力分布。换句话说，AI 让主体更容易把握客体，也可能悄悄限定主体究竟只能以什么方式去把握客体。正因为这两面性同时存在，AI for Science 才不能被简单说成是工具升级，而应被理解为一种改变认知路径的中介条件。
030 [Normal] 三、理论、数据与实验关系的重组
031 [Normal] 把问题进一步放到理论、数据与实验三者的关系上，这种变化会显得更清楚。借用库恩关于范式转换的讨论来理解当前情形[2]，我们看到的并不是科研只是在原有轨道上局部提速，而是研究组织方式本身在发生结构性调整。传统科学实践当然也存在反复往返，但长期以来，理论提出假说、实验提供检验、数据作为结果证据的基本格局始终比较稳定。今天真正变化的，是三者之间的先后顺序、权重配置以及彼此耦合的方式。
032 [Normal] 最先发生变化的，是数据的位置。过去，数据更多在研究后段作为结果材料出现；现在，它越来越像研究得以启动的前提条件。模型之所以能够预测蛋白质构象、生成材料候选或捕捉潜在反应路径，首先是因为大量已有数据已经被整理成可计算的形式。尤其是文献嵌入和数据库学习的普遍使用，使既有知识不再只是供研究者阅读的文本和图表，也作为训练样本和表示空间的一部分，提前规定了模型能够“看见”什么[10]。
033 [Normal] 与此同时，模型也不再只是一个算得更快的辅助部件。它更像夹在数据与实验之间的中间层：一端从既有数据中提取特征、压缩空间，另一端又把候选排序、性质预测和参数建议送回实验环节。正因为模型嵌在这两个方向之间，研究流程才越来越不像几步顺次展开的线性过程，而更像一个预测、验证、再训练不断往复的循环。
034 [Normal] 实验的位置也因此发生了转移。模型能力增强，并没有让实验失去价值，反而让实验的职责变得更集中。越来越多的研究不再从大范围盲试起步，而是先由模型压缩候选空间，再把有限的实验资源投向关键变量和异常结果。这样一来，实验不只是结论最后的确认环节，而是持续参与模型修正、结果校准和研究方向调整的反馈机制。
035 [Normal] 但这里最不能被忽略的，恰恰还是理论。现实情况并不是理论被数据淹没了，而是理论换了位置。一方面，它继续为对象表征、变量选择、目标设定和结果判别提供边界，防止模型在缺少学科约束的情况下盲目搜索；另一方面，模型给出的异常候选、反常关联和失败结果，又会反过来逼着理论修正原有解释。于是，理论、数据与实验不再表现为相对分段的三步，而更像一个不断往返、彼此校正的循环回路。与其说是“数据取代理论”或“模型替代实验”，不如说三者之间形成了一种新的协同结构。
036 [Normal] 四、科学家主体性的迁移与重塑
037 [Normal] 随着模型和自动化平台越来越深地嵌入科研流程，常有人担心科学家会在发现过程中被边缘化。至少就现阶段来看，问题并不在于科学主体会不会被简单替代，而在于其工作重心已经发生转移。过去大量时间花在候选搜寻、重复试错、人工筛查和技术调试上；如今，这些流程的一部分正被模型和平台接管，但问题设定是否准确、异常结果是否值得追问、机制解释能否成立、结论应当说到什么程度，反而更依赖研究者的判断。
038 [Normal] 但工作重心的转移并不自动等于主体性增强。若研究者只是顺着系统给出的排序、推荐和默认路径往前走，科研实践就可能从“人使用工具”慢慢滑向“人服从平台逻辑”。这种削弱并不表现为科学家不在场，而是表现在很多本该由人承担的判断，已经在平台规则中被预先塑形了。真正需要警惕的，不是人有没有留在环路里，而是关键判断权是否还牢牢掌握在研究者自己手中。
039 [Normal] 所以，在 AI 条件下谈科学主体性，关键并不在于研究者是否重新掌握了每一道技术细节，而在于他是否还能对整套中介系统保持稳定的判断力和批判力。训练数据有没有系统偏差，目标函数是否真的对应研究问题，统计显著会不会被误当成机制重要，异常结果有没有在过滤过程中被自动清除，结论究竟应当说到什么强度，这些都不能交给平台默认处理。换句话说，科学家并没有因为 AI 的加入而“变轻”，只是主体性的内容从操作层面更多转到了判断层面和责任层面。
040 [Normal] 五、典型案例中的范式变动
041 [Normal] 这些讨论如果只停留在概念层面，多少会显得有些抽象。若从近几年几篇最有代表性的顶刊论文切入，问题会更容易看清。下文主要选取 AlphaFold 改变结构生物学起点的研究[3]、GNoME 重组材料搜索空间的研究[5]、自主实验室进入无机材料合成流程的研究[6]，以及大语言模型参与数学发现的研究[9]，来具体说明 AI 如何改变研究起点、证据组织方式以及协作结构。
042 [Normal] 以 AlphaFold 为例，Jumper 等人的工作之所以重要，不只是因为它把蛋白质结构预测精度推到了一个新高度，更因为它悄悄改写了结构生物学的研究起点[3]。过去，很多工作往往要先花费大量时间获得结构线索，后续功能分析和机制解释才能展开；而 AlphaFold 提供了足够强的先验结构信息，使不少研究可以先从模型预测形成初步假设，再把实验资源集中到功能验证、机制分析和边界条件检验上。研究起点的变化，本身就说明模型已经进入了知识生产链条的前端。
043 [Normal] 材料发现中的变化也很典型。Merchant 等人关于 GNoME 的研究表明，深度学习模型的价值并不只在于“多找出一些候选晶体”，更在于它先替研究者压缩了一个原本几乎无法直接穷举的巨大搜索空间[5]。一旦这一前置工作交给模型完成，后续实验的方向性就会显著增强。换言之，模型不再只是把既有步骤做得更快，而是在前端就参与了“哪些对象值得先做”的判断。
044 [Normal] 再看自主实验室的案例，这种平台化趋势会更明显。Szymanski 等人的研究表明，模型提出候选、数据库累计历史结果、实验装置执行合成、反馈系统再把新结果及时送回模型，这几个环节已经可以被接成相对连续的闭环[6]。如果把 Burger 等关于移动机器人化学家的工作一并考虑进来，就会更清楚地看到，这类系统并不是单点自动化，而是在向平台化实验组织演化[7]。当这种结构真正运转起来时，科研活动就很难再被描述为理论、实验和分析的简单串联，它更像是一个由多种技术中介共同维持的连续回路。
045 [Normal] 数学案例提供了另一个重要侧面。Romera-Paredes 等人与 Davies 等人的研究都表明，大语言模型与程序搜索已经能够在数学问题中参与模式识别、猜想生成乃至启发证明路径的发现[8][9]。这当然不意味着机器已经拥有与数学家等量齐观的理解力，但它至少说明，“先发现什么值得证明”这一步正在被重新组织，而这恰恰是过去通常被看作最依赖人类直觉的环节。
046 [Normal] 把这些案例并列起来看，一个共同点会变得很明显：AI for Science 真正改变的，不只是答案出现得更快，而是问题如何被排列、候选如何被筛出、实验如何被调用。也正是在这个意义上，人工智能进入科学发现过程，不应只被理解为工具升级，而更接近一种知识生产范式的结构性变化。
047 [Normal] 不过，流程被重组，并不等于理解就会自动增长。AI 越深入科学发现，越有必要继续追问一个老问题：预测成功，到底能不能直接等同于科学理解的增长。这个区分如果不做清楚，很多看似耀眼的成果都可能停留在“有效”而非“被理解”的层面。
048 [Normal] 六、AI for Science 的认识论限度
049 [Normal] 讨论到这里，认识论上的问题就不能回避了。Krenn 等人特别强调，科学理解并不只取决于结果是否命中，还取决于研究者能否说明其成立条件、适用边界以及它与既有理论之间的关系[11]。顺着这一点往下看，AI for Science 目前最突出的长处，确实是搜索能力和关联能力的大幅提高，但这并不意味着机制解释已经同步成熟。
050 [Normal] 对基础研究来说，这个区分尤其不能被轻轻带过。模型很擅长从复杂数据里抓住相关结构，可真正的科学解释往往还要继续回答机制、因果和边界条件这些更难的问题。如果共同体过早把高命中率直接换算成高理解力，表面上像是方法进步，实际上却可能压缩理论阐释和反思的空间。
051 [Normal] 还有一个容易被忽视的地方，是模型处理的知识来源本身并不透明。Messeri 与 Crockett 之所以有启发性，就在于他们提醒研究者警惕一种“理解幻象”[12]。已有文献、数据库和实验记录在进入模型之前，就已经带着学科共同体长期积累下来的关注焦点、分类方式和研究盲区。当模型输出足够复杂、结果又足够显著时，研究者便很容易误以为自己已经真正把握了对象。问题未必出在模型“没用”，而更可能出在我们过早把有效预测等同于充分认识。
052 [Normal] 说到底，AI 眼下最突出的能力，仍然是快速搜索、压缩空间和重组线索，而不是自己给出机制说明。它当然能够帮助研究者更快逼近值得研究的问题，可一旦涉及“为什么成立”，最后仍然离不开理论判断、实验验证和解释工作。若把这两类能力混成一回事，很多所谓突破就容易停在方法成功的层面。
053 [Normal] 也正因为如此，治理问题不能被放到技术成熟之后再来补课。如果 AI for Science 已经进入知识生产内部，那么治理本身就是新范式能否成立的条件之一。它不属于外围修饰，而是这套结构能否长期稳定运转的内部要求。
054 [Normal] 首先要重新审视的，其实是评价尺度。现在很多研究过于看重最优结果、最高命中率和最漂亮的性能表格，而对解释是否充分、失败是否被报告、结论边界是否被说明、结果能否被复核，重视明显不够。时间一长，科研共同体就很容易被“可发表的漂亮结果”牵着走。
055 [Normal] 如果资源分配始终沿着单一性能逻辑展开，最先被挤压的往往不是短期成果，而是机制解释、失败报告和边界条件研究。久而久之，论文叙述、经费配置乃至研究议程都会越来越围绕“能不能出结果”展开，而不是“我们到底理解了什么”。
056 [Normal] 因此，在本文看来，治理并不是 AI for Science 之外的附属议题，而是这套新知识生产结构能否稳住自身秩序的内部条件。若对平台逻辑、责任分配和评价机制缺少同步调整，模型能力越强，科研秩序反而越可能被单一性能导向牵着走。
057 [Normal] 还需要补充的一点，是公平问题。Gao 与 Wang 的研究提醒我们，AI 的扩散不仅改变了科研产出的数量，也在重新分配科研影响力和先发优势[13]。谁能够稳定获得高质量数据、充足算力和平台接入权限，决定的已经不只是研究效率，还决定着谁更容易进入新的科研范式并参与规则塑造。如果这种结构长期固化，那么 AI for Science 带来的就不只是能力提升，也可能是知识生产不平等的进一步放大。

013 [Normal] 摘要：这几年，AI for Science 已经不再只是技术宣传里的热词，而是真正进入科研现场的一种新变量。很多讨论首先看到的是算力、模型和自动化实验带来的提速效果，但本文更关心另一层问题：当模型、数据和实验开始重新嵌进彼此的工作流程时，科学知识究竟是在什么意义上被生产出来的。本文借助自然辩证法关于实践、中介与主体客体关系的分析框架，讨论 AI for Science 对科学发现方式带来的结构性影响。本文认为，关键变化不在于机器会不会替代科学家，也不在于数据是否压倒理论，而在于理论、数据和实验原有的分工秩序正在被重
014 [Normal] 关键词：AI for Science；自然辩证法；科学知识生产；科学智能；人机协同；科研治理
016 [Normal] 引言
017 [Normal] 过去几年，人工智能进入基础科研的速度比许多人预想得更快。AlphaFold 改变了蛋白质结构研究的起点，材料发现越来越依赖模型先行压缩搜索空间，数学研究也开始明显感受到大模型和程序搜索带来的启发作用[3][5][9]。把这些进展放在一起看，一个事实已经很难回避：人工智能不再只是科研外围的辅助算力，它正逐步进入发现过程本身。
018 [Normal] 围绕这一变化，近几年的顶刊讨论其实已经形成了几条彼此勾连的线索。Wang 等人强调，AI for Science 的意义在于模型、数据与自动化实验正在共同改造科学发现的基础设施[1]；Krenn 等人提醒人们，预测更准并不等于理解更深[11]；Messeri 与 Crockett 则进一步指出，若研究者过早把模型输出当成“已经理解”，就可能落入一种解释贫乏却看似成功的幻象[12]。这些研究放在一起看，真正值得追问的已经不只是效率，而是科学研究内部的认识结构有没有被改写。
019 [Normal] 现有讨论的一个明显不足，是不少分析停留在应用层面：要么把 AI 看成更强的科研工具，要么直接把它想象成替代性主体。本文更关心中间层的问题，也就是模型进入发现过程之后，理论、数据、实验和科学家判断之间的关系如何改变。把这个问题放回自然辩证法的视野，我们看到的就不只是技术升级，而是主体、客体与中介关系的再组织。本文希望讨论的，正是这种再组织的知识论含义及其治理后果。
020 [Normal] 一、问题的提出：AI for Science 不应被简化为效率工具
021 [Normal] 如果只说 AI for Science 让科研更快，这个判断当然有道理，但还不够。蛋白质结构预测、药物发现和材料设计这些领域都说明，模型确实大幅压缩了高维搜索所耗费的时间，也提高了候选排序的效率[3][4][5]。可科学研究毕竟不是一场单纯的提速竞赛。结果来得再快，若不能进入解释、复核和共同体认可的链条，就很难真正变成有分量的知识。正因如此，AI for Science 更值得被理解为一种可能改变研究秩序的知识条件。

    ns={'a':'http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/main'}
    for si,n in enumerate(slide_names,1):

        title=texts[0] if texts else ''
        print(si, title[:80], '|', ' / '.join(texts[1:5])[:140])

17 Normal align JUSTIFY (3) first_line_cm 0.85 line_spacing 1.5 text 过去几年，人工智能进入基础科研的速度比许多人预想得更快。AlphaFold 改变了蛋白质结构研究的起点，材料发现越来越依赖模型先行压缩搜索空间，数学研究也开始明 fonts [('Times New Roman', 12.0, None)]
18 Normal align JUSTIFY (3) first_line_cm 0.85 line_spacing 1.5 text 围绕这一变化，近几年的顶刊讨论其实已经形成了几条彼此勾连的线索。Wang 等人强调，AI for Science 的意义在于模型、数据与自动化实验正在共同改造科 fonts [('Times New Roman', 12.0, None)]
19 Normal align JUSTIFY (3) first_line_cm 0.85 line_spacing 1.5 text 现有讨论的一个明显不足，是不少分析停留在应用层面：要么把 AI 看成更强的科研工具，要么直接把它想象成替代性主体。本文更关心中间层的问题，也就是模型进入发现过程 fonts [('Times New Roman', 12.0, None)]
20 Normal align JUSTIFY (3) first_line_cm None line_spacing 1.5 text 一、问题的提出：AI for Science 不应被简化为效率工具 fonts [('Times New Roman', 14.0, True)]
21 Normal align JUSTIFY (3) first_line_cm 0.85 line_spacing 1.5 text 如果只说 AI for Science 让科研更快，这个判断当然有道理，但还不够。蛋白质结构预测、药物发现和材料设计这些领域都说明，模型确实大幅压缩了高维搜索所 fonts [('Times New Roman', 12.0, None)]

23 Normal align JUSTIFY (3) first_line_cm 0.85 line_spacing 1.5 text 因此，真正值得讨论的并不是效率提升本身，而是知识生产链条有没有被改写。过去，理论、数据与实验虽然并不总是严格线性推进，但分工大体稳定：理论提出解释框架和假设，实 fonts [('Times New Roman', 12.0, None)]
24 Normal align JUSTIFY (3) first_line_cm 0.85 line_spacing 1.5 text 若把这种变化放回自然辩证法的视野，问题就不能只理解成“技术有没有用”。更值得追问的是，当模型成为研究者接近对象的前置环节之后，人和对象究竟通过什么方式建立联系， fonts [('Times New Roman', 12.0, None)]

⼆、AI作为认知中介及主体客体关系的再组织
该段落可能为AI⽣成的概率为：25.2%
摘要：近⼏年，AI for Science 已不再只是技术宣传中的热词，⽽是切实进⼊科研组织内部的现实⼒量。围绕这⼀变化，现有讨论往往⾸先强调算⼒增⻓、模型性能和⾃动化实验带来的提速效果。本⽂更想追问的是，当模型、数据与实验被重新编织在⼀起时，科学知识究竟是在什么意义上被⽣产出来的。 借助⾃然辩证法关于实践、中介与主体客体关系的分析框架，并结合 Wang 等、Krenn 等、Messeri 与 Crockett 等关于科学智能、科学理解
也正因为如此，AI for Science 已经形成了相当有分量的讨论场域。Wang 等⼈把它概括为⼈⼯智能时代科学发现的总体转向，强调模型、数据和⾃动化实验正在合并为新的发现基础设施[1]；Krenn 等⼈则提醒⼈们，预测能⼒的提升并不⾃动等于科学理解的增⻓[11]；Messeri 与 Crockett 更进⼀步指出，当研究者把复杂模型输出直接当成“已经理解”，就可能陷⼊⼀种⽅法成功掩盖解释贫乏的幻象[12]。这些判断并不⽭盾，反⽽共
现有讨论的⼀个明显不⾜，是不少分析停留在应⽤层⾯：要么把 AI 看成更强的科研⼯具，要么直接把它想象成替代性主体。本⽂更关⼼中间层的问题，也就是模型进⼊发现过程之后，理论、数据、实验和科学家判断之间的关系如何改变。把这个问题放回⾃然辩证法的视野，我们看到的就不只是技术升级，⽽是主体、客体与中介关系的再组织。本⽂希望讨论的，正是这种再组织的知识论含义及其治理后果。
如果只说 AI for Science 让科研更快，这个判断当然不能算错，但它只触及了表层。⽆论是蛋⽩质结构预测、药物筛选还是材料设计，模型的确明显压缩了⾼维搜索所需要的时间，也提升了候选排序的效率[1][3][4][5]。可问题在于，科学研究不是⼀般意义上的提速竞赛。结果再快、命中率再⾼，若不能进⼊解释、复核和共同体承认的链条，就很难真正转化为有分量的知识。也正因为如此，AI for Science 更值得被看作⼀种可能改写研究秩序的
因此，真正值得讨论的并不是效率提升本身，⽽是知识⽣产链条有没有被改写。过去，理论、数据与实验虽然并⾮严格线性排列，但⼤致分⼯仍然相对稳定：理论提出解释框架和假设，实验承担检验，数据更多作为结果证据进⼊分析。现在情况正在变化。数据越来越早地进⼊对象表征和模型训练，模型开始参与候选⽣成与研究路径压缩，实验则更多承担反馈、校正和纠偏的功能。也就是说，AI for Science 触动的不是某⼀个环节的增强，⽽是科学发现内部⼯作秩序的重新安排。
若把这⼀变化放回⾃然辩证法的视野，问题就不能只理解为“技术有没有⽤”。更关键的是，当模型开始成为研究者接近对象的前置环节时，⼈和对象之间究竟通过什么⽅式发⽣联系，知识⼜是在何种中介链条中被组织出来。效率提升当然重要，但若只把 AI for Science 看成科研加速器，我们就容易忽略它对认识路径、证据组织⽅式以及科研分⼯结构带来的更深层改动。

### Word-compatible tables

- Use tables only for tabular information, not as divider lines, spacing hacks, or two-column text layout. Use paragraph borders, tab stops, or proper headers/footers for rules and alignment.
- Use DXA table widths only. Do not use percentage widths for generated tables.
- Standard content tables and metadata tables should default to full content width. Under the default page setup, use 9360 DXA.
- Align tables flush with the body text column and nearby subheaders by default. A full-width table should start at the same left edge as the section text and span the content width; do not center tables or add extra left indentation unless the user asks for it.
- The acceptance check is the rendered outer table border, not just the XML. If Word or LibreOffice renders a nominally left-aligned table a little left or right of the text column, adjust the explicit table indent/alignment until the visible table border is flush with the subheader/body left edge.
- Use narrower tables only when the user asks for a compact object or the table is intentionally not a primary content table.
- Choose column widths by content. Short fields such as status, date, owner, score, yes/no, and IDs should be compact; narrative columns should get the remaining width.
- After all rows are created, normalize the table geometry so `tblW`, `tblGrid`, and every row's `tcW` agree. The table width must equal the sum of grid column widths, and each cell width must match its column.
- In Python, use `scripts/table_geometry.py` for this normalization. Build the table rows first, compute exact DXA column widths with `column_widths_from_weights(...)` or `exact_column_widths(...)`, then call `apply_table_geometry(table, widths, table_width_dxa=sum(widths), indent_dxa=0)`. This is the python-docx equivalent of the docx-js `width` + `columnWidths` + cell `width` pattern: it writes `tblW`, `tblGrid/gridCol`, every `tcW`, fixed table layout, left alignment, and cell margins together.
- Do not rely on autofit to rescue bad geometry. Prefer fixed, explicit widths that Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice, and Codex preview can all interpret conservatively.
- Add cell margins/padding on every table. A good default is 80 DXA top/bottom and 120 DXA left/right, adjusted upward when the table feels cramped.
- Never set fixed row heights that can clip text. Let rows expand, use readable wrapping, and reduce font size only after width and wrapping choices are correct.
- For multi-page tables, repeat the header row and keep the same column order and widths across page breaks.
- Default visual treatment is a simple full-width grid: white body cells, thin light-gray borders, dark body text, and no zebra striping.
- Prefer a plain built-in Word table style such as `Table Grid` as the baseline. Use a lightly shaded header row only when it stays subtle; do not use saturated dark header bars, heavy fills, or blue body text unless the user asks for a branded design.
- Header rows should use modest bold text and either white fill or a very light tint. Borders should remain thin and quiet.
- For document metadata near the title, prefer a full-width metadata table with compact labels, comfortable padding, consistent column widths, and the same simple grid treatment. Avoid multicolor label bands by default.

### Word-compatible lists

- Never create fake lists with Unicode bullets, hyphen-prefixed bullets, manually typed numbers, or newline-separated items inside one paragraph.
- Use real Word numbering/list paragraphs for bullets and numbered lists.
- Default list indent: marker position 360 DXA from the body left edge; item text starts at 720 DXA with a 360 DXA hanging indent. This creates equal left-side air before the marker and between the marker and text, so the bullet circle is indented relative to the subheading instead of sitting on the same left edge.
- The first list item must use the same real list style and indentation as the rest of the list. It must not sit flush with the heading or body left edge.
- Prefer a small, light bullet marker from a real Word list style. Do not type oversized manual bullet characters into the paragraph text.
- Make each list item its own paragraph, including list items inside table cells.
- Use the same list definition when numbering should continue. Use a separate list definition only when numbering should restart.
- Keep list spacing compatible with body text unless the document style calls for tighter or looser spacing.

#### List rhythm and spacing

- Give the list lead-in or subheading clear separation from the first item; lists should not feel pinned to the title above them.
- Default list lead-in rhythm: keep about 32px of rendered vertical space after the lead-in/subheading before the first bullet.
- Default list-item rhythm: tune paragraph spacing so the rendered gap between consecutive bullet items is about 32px. Start with 0pt before / 8pt after at the default render scale, then adjust after visual QA if the rendered PNG does not show roughly 32px.
- Use the same 32px rendered gap for executive-facing or skim-first documents unless the user asks for a looser list.
- Do not let same-style/contextual spacing suppression collapse the gap between consecutive list items. If the renderer shows much more or less than 32px between bullets, adjust paragraph-after spacing until the rendered page matches the 32px target.
- Do not insert blank paragraphs between bullets. Use paragraph spacing on the list style.
- Wrapped bullet lines must align under the item text, not under the bullet marker.

### Structural QA before final render review

Before the final render-and-visual review, inspect or audit the DOCX for common construction mistakes:

- Fake bullets, hyphen bullets, manually typed numbering, or multi-item lists inside one paragraph.
- Missing explicit page size or margins.
- Fake headings made from Normal paragraphs with direct formatting.
- Heading styles missing outline levels when TOC/navigation behavior matters.
- Tables missing explicit width, grid columns, or cell widths.
- Tables with percentage widths, inconsistent `tblW` / `tblGrid` / `tcW`, or total width beyond the page margins.
- Tables that have not passed `python scripts/table_geometry.py <docx>` or an equivalent structural audit after generation.
- Table cells missing margins/padding, text pinned to borders, fixed row heights, or missing repeated header rows on multi-page tables.
- Divider or layout tables that should be paragraph borders, tab stops, section structure, or header/footer content instead.
- Heavy table styling by default: saturated dark headers, zebra striping, colored body text, multicolor metadata labels, or thick borders.
- Cramped lists, bullets stuck too close to the heading above, oversized bullet markers, bullet markers flush with the heading/body left edge, first bullets with different indentation from the rest of the list, rendered table borders offset from the subheader/body left edge, tables that are centered/indented instead of flush with the subheader/body left edge, tables that do not use full width without a clear reason, or inconsistent/missing running headers.

[12] 当科学发现开始依赖模型：自然辩证法视域下AI for Science的知识生产重组
[13] 摘要：这几年，AI for Science 已经不再只是技术宣传里的热词，而是真正进入科研现场的一种新变量。很多讨论首先看到的是算力、模型和自动化实验带来的提速效果，但本文更关心另一层问题：当模型、数据和实验开始重新嵌进彼此的工作流程时，科学知识究竟是在什么意义上被生产出来的。本文借助自然辩证法关于实践、中介与主体客体关系的分析框架，讨论 AI for Science 对科学发现方式带来的结构性影响。本文认为，关键变化不在于机器会不会替代科学家，也不在于数据是否压倒理论，而在于理论、数据和实验原有的分工秩序正在被重新安排。数据更早进入研究起点，模型更深地卷入对象表征和候选生成，实验则更多承担验证、校准和纠偏任务。相应地，科学家的作用并没有消失，而是更集中地体现在问题设定、结果解释与责任判断上。如果评价仍主要围绕预测精度和筛选效率展开，那么解释不足、平台黑箱、责任稀释以及科研资源再集中等问题就容易被遮蔽。基于此，本文主张把 AI for Science 看作科学知识生产方式的一次结构性重组，并以解释力、可复核性和制度正当性作为更合适的评价标准。
[14] 关键词：AI for Science；自然辩证法；科学知识生产；科学智能；人机协同；科研治理
[16] 引言
[17] 过去几年，人工智能进入基础科研的速度比许多人预想得更快。AlphaFold 改变了蛋白质结构研究的起点，材料发现越来越依赖模型先行压缩搜索空间，数学研究也开始明显感受到大模型和程序搜索带来的启发作用[3][5][9]。把这些进展放在一起看，一个事实已经很难回避：人工智能不再只是科研外围的辅助算力，它正逐步进入发现过程本身。
[18] 围绕这一变化，近几年的顶刊讨论其实已经形成了几条彼此勾连的线索。Wang 等人强调，AI for Science 的意义在于模型、数据与自动化实验正在共同改造科学发现的基础设施[1]；Krenn 等人提醒人们，预测更准并不等于理解更深[11]；Messeri 与 Crockett 则进一步指出，若研究者过早把模型输出当成“已经理解”，就可能落入一种解释贫乏却看似成功的幻象[12]。这些研究放在一起看，真正值得追问的已经不只是效率，而是科学研究内部的认识结构有没有被改写。
[19] 现有讨论的一个明显不足，是不少分析停留在应用层面：要么把 AI 看成更强的科研工具，要么直接把它想象成替代性主体。本文更关心中间层的问题，也就是模型进入发现过程之后，理论、数据、实验和科学家判断之间的关系如何改变。把这个问题放回自然辩证法的视野，我们看到的就不只是技术升级，而是主体、客体与中介关系的再组织。本文希望讨论的，正是这种再组织的知识论含义及其治理后果。
[20] 一、问题的提出：AI for Science 不应被简化为效率工具
[21] 如果只说 AI for Science 让科研更快，这个判断当然有道理，但还不够。蛋白质结构预测、药物发现和材料设计这些领域都说明，模型确实大幅压缩了高维搜索所耗费的时间，也提高了候选排序的效率[3][4][5]。可科学研究毕竟不是一场单纯的提速竞赛。结果来得再快，若不能进入解释、复核和共同体认可的链条，就很难真正变成有分量的知识。正因如此，AI for Science 更值得被理解为一种可能改变研究秩序的知识条件。
[22] 问题恰恰就在这里。科学研究从来不是把一个最优解算出来就算结束，它还要求研究者说明结果为什么成立、适用到哪里为止，又怎样和既有理论接起来。换句话说，科学发现既是技术过程，也是知识过程；既涉及性能指标，也涉及机制解释；既依赖实验与计算，也受制于共同体对“什么能够算作证据”的集体判断。把这一层抽掉，只剩效率，科学活动最关键的部分反而看不见了。
[23] 因此，真正值得讨论的并不是效率提升本身，而是知识生产链条有没有被改写。过去，理论、数据与实验虽然并不总是严格线性推进，但分工大体稳定：理论提出解释框架和假设，实验承担检验，数据更多作为结果证据进入分析。现在这种格局正在松动。数据…4737 chars truncated…和最漂亮的性能表格，而对解释是否充分、失败是否被报告、结论边界是否被说明、结果能否被复核，重视明显不够。时间一长，科研共同体就很容易被“可发表的漂亮结果”牵着走。
[55] 如果资源分配始终沿着单一性能逻辑展开，最先被挤压的往往不是短期成果，而是机制解释、失败报告和边界条件研究。久而久之，论文叙述、经费配置乃至研究议程都会越来越围绕“能不能出结果”展开，而不是“我们到底理解了什么”。
[56] 因此，在本文看来，治理并不是 AI for Science 之外的附属议题，而是这套新知识生产结构能否稳住自身秩序的内部条件。若对平台逻辑、责任分配和评价机制缺少同步调整，模型能力越强，科研秩序反而越可能被单一性能导向牵着走。
[57] 还需要补充的一点，是公平问题。Gao 与 Wang 的研究提醒我们，AI 的扩散不仅改变了科研产出的数量，也在重新分配科研影响力和先发优势[13]。谁能够稳定获得高质量数据、充足算力和平台接入权限，决定的已经不只是研究效率，还决定着谁更容易进入新的科研范式并参与规则塑造。如果这种结构长期固化，那么 AI for Science 带来的就不只是能力提升，也可能是知识生产不平等的进一步放大。
[58] 结语
[59] 回过头看，AI for Science 的意义显然不能被压缩成一套单纯的提效叙事。更深的变化在于，人工智能正在重新安排对象如何被表征、证据如何被组织、结论又如何被确认。由此被改变的，不只是理论、数据与实验的配合方式，也是科学家在其中承担的角色、责任和判断位置。
[60] 从自然辩证法的立场看，AI for Science 更像是科学认识中介的一次明显扩展。中介一旦扩展，人类确实更容易进入复杂问题空间，也更有可能在更短时间内找到有效候选；但这并不意味着理解本身会自动加深。中介越强，新的黑箱、依赖关系和资源不平等也可能越突出。因此，评价 AI for Science 不能只停在性能数字上，还必须把解释性、可复核性、责任归属和公平性放在一起考虑。
[61] 因此，本文更愿意把 AI for Science 看成一种仍在形成中的科学新条件，而不是已经完全定型的成功范式。它能否从一轮技术热潮真正沉淀为稳定的科学能力，最终取决于三件事能否一起推进：认识论上的反思，方法论上的调整，以及制度层面的治理。把这三者放到同一问题框架里讨论，也正是自然辩证法在今天仍然具有现实意义的原因。

[26] 自然辩证法早就提醒我们，科学认识并不是主体对客体的直接照面，而总是通过一系列中介逐步展开。实验装置、数学模型、测量技术、符号系统乃至协作网络，都在其中起作用。很多时候，科学史上真正重要的跃迁，并不是对象自己忽然“显露出来”，而是人类找到了新的中介，因而获得了接近对象的新路径。
[27] 把 AI 放进这个脉络里看，它之所以不同于一般计算工具，不只是因为算得更快，而是因为它同时介入了表征、筛选、生成和反馈几个环节。对象一旦被转写成可计算的表示，模型就不再只是被动执行命令，而开始参与判断什么值得关注、什么应当优先实验、哪些异常需要继续追问。从这个意义上说，AI 已经不只是流程中的一个部件，而是在一定程度上改写了发现流程本身。
[28] 更进一步说，被改写的还不只是流程，而是研究者接近对象的方式。传统实验科学里，主体主要借助观察、测量和操控来面对对象；而在 AI for Science 的场景中，对象往往要先被处理成序列、图结构、晶体表示或反应网络，然后才进入模型空间接受比较、排序和预测。主体与客体之间因此多出了一层由数据集、表征方案、损失函数、搜索策略和平台规则共同构成的中介。对象不再只以自然存在者的形态出现，也以可计算表征的形式进入研究；研究者的工作则更多转向数据治理、模型审查和解释责任承担。
[29] 当然，中介增多不只意味着能力扩展，也带来新的约束。模型确实让研究者能够进入原本难以处理的高维问题空间，但它同时也会借助训练数据的边界、目标函数的设定以及平台规则的偏好，重新安排研究者的注意力分布。换句话说，AI 让主体更容易把握客体，也可能悄悄限定主体究竟只能以什么方式去把握客体。正因为这两面性同时存在，AI for Science 才不能被简单说成是工具升级，而应被理解为一种改变认知路径的中介条件。
[30] 三、理论、数据与实验关系的重组
[31] 把问题进一步放到理论、数据与实验三者的关系上，这种变化会显得更清楚。借用库恩关于范式转换的讨论来理解当前情形[2]，我们看到的并不是科研只是在原有轨道上局部提速，而是研究组织方式本身在发生结构性调整。传统科学实践当然也存在反复往返，但长期以来，理论提出假说、实验提供检验、数据作为结果证据的基本格局始终比较稳定。今天真正变化的，是三者之间的先后顺序、权重配置以及彼此耦合的方式。
[32] 最先发生变化的，是数据的位置。过去，数据更多在研究后段作为结果材料出现；现在，它越来越像研究得以启动的前提条件。模型之所以能够预测蛋白质构象、生成材料候选或捕捉潜在反应路径，首先是因为大量已有数据已经被整理成可计算的形式。尤其是文献嵌入和数据库学习的普遍使用，使既有知识不再只是供研究者阅读的文本和图表，也作为训练样本和表示空间的一部分，提前规定了模型能够“看见”什么[10]。
[33] 与此同时，模型也不再只是一个算得更快的辅助部件。它更像夹在数据与实验之间的中间层：一端从既有数据中提取特征、压缩空间，另一端又把候选排序、性质预测和参数建议送回实验环节。正因为模型嵌在这两个方向之间，研究流程才越来越不像几步顺次展开的线性过程，而更像一个预测、验证、再训练不断往复的循环。
[34] 实验的位置也因此发生了转移。模型能力增强，并没有让实验失去价值，反而让实验的职责变得更集中。越来越多的研究不再从大范围盲试起步，而是先由模型压缩候选空间，再把有限的实验资源投向关键变量和异常结果。这样一来，实验不只是结论最后的确认环节，而是持续参与模型修正、结果校准和研究方向调整的反馈机制。
[35] 但这里最不能被忽略的，恰恰还是理论。现实情况并不是理论被数据淹没了，而是理论换了位置。一方面，它继续为对象表征、变量选择、目标设定和结果判别提供边界，防止模型在缺少学科约束的情况下盲目搜索；另一方面，模型给出的异常候选、反常关联和失败结果，又会反过来逼着理论修正原有解释。于是，理论、数据与实验不再表现为相对分段的三步，而更像一个不断往返、彼此校正的循环回路。与其说是“数据取代理论”或“模型替代实验”，不如说三者之间形成了一种新的协同结构。
[36] 四、科学家主体性的迁移与重塑
[37] 随着模型和自动化平台越来越深地嵌入科研流程，常有人担心科学家会在发现过程中被边缘化。至少就现阶段来看，问题并不在于科学主体会不会被简单替代，而在于其工作重心已经发生转移。过去大量时间花在候选搜寻、重复试错、人工筛查和技术调试上；如今，这些流程的一部分正被模型和平台接管，但问题设定是否准确、异常结果是否值得追问、机制解释能否成立、结论应当说到什么程度，反而更依赖研究者的判断。
[38] 但工作重心的转移并不自动等于主体性增强。若研究者只是顺着系统给出的排序、推荐和默认路径往前走，科研实践就可能从“人使用工具”慢慢滑向“人服从平台逻辑”。这种削弱并不表现为科学家不在场，而是表现在很多本该由人承担的判断，已经在平台规则中被预先塑形了。真正需要警惕的，不是人有没有留在环路里，而是关键判断权是否还牢牢掌握在研究者自己手中。
[39] 所以，在 AI 条件下谈科学主体性，关键并不在于研究者是否重新掌握了每一道技术细节，而在于他是否还能对整套中介系统保持稳定的判断力和批判力。训练数据有没有系统偏差，目标函数是否真的对应研究问题，统计显著会不会被误当成机制重要，异常结果有没有在过滤过程中被自动清除，结论究竟应当说到什么强度，这些都不能交给平台默认处理。换句话说，科学家并没有因为 AI 的加入而“变轻”，只是主体性的内容从操作层面更多转到了判断层面和责任层面。
[40] 五、典型案例中的范式变动
[41] 这些讨论如果只停留在概念层面，多少会显得有些抽象。若从近几年几篇最有代表性的顶刊论文切入，问题会更容易看清。下文主要选取 AlphaFold 改变结构生物学起点的研究[3]、GNoME 重组材料搜索空间的研究[5]、自主实验室进入无机材料合成流程的研究[6]，以及大语言模型参与数学发现的研究[9]，来具体说明 AI 如何改变研究起点、证据组织方式以及协作结构。
[42] 以 AlphaFold 为例，Jumper 等人的工作之所以重要，不只是因为它把蛋白质结构预测精度推到了一个新高度，更因为它悄悄改写了结构生物学的研究起点[3]。过去，很多工作往往要先花费大量时间获得结构线索，后续功能分析和机制解释才能展开；而 AlphaFold 提供了足够强的先验结构信息，使不少研究可以先从模型预测形成初步假设，再把实验资源集中到功能验证、机制分析和边界条件检验上。研究起点的变化，本身就说明模型已经进入了知识生产链条的前端。
[43] 材料发现中的变化也很典型。Merchant 等人关于 GNoME 的研究表明，深度学习模型的价值并不只在于“多找出一些候选晶体”，更在于它先替研究者压缩了一个原本几乎无法直接穷举的巨大搜索空间[5]。一旦这一前置工作交给模型完成，后续实验的方向性就会显著增强。换言之，模型不再只是把既有步骤做得更快，而是在前端就参与了“哪些对象值得先做”的判断。
[44] 再看自主实验室的案例，这种平台化趋势会更明显。Szymanski 等人的研究表明，模型提出候选、数据库累计历史结果、实验装置执行合成、反馈系统再把新结果及时送回模型，这几个环节已经可以被接成相对连续的闭环[6]。如果把 Burger 等关于移动机器人化学家的工作一并考虑进来，就会更清楚地看到，这类系统并不是单点自动化，而是在向平台化实验组织演化[7]。当这种结构真正运转起来时，科研活动就很难再被描述为理论、实验和分析的简单串联，它更像是一个由多种技术中介共同维持的连续回路。
[45] 数学案例提供了另一个重要侧面。Romera-Paredes 等人与 Davies 等人的研究都表明，大语言模型与程序搜索已经能够在数学问题中参与模式识别、猜想生成乃至启发证明路径的发现[8][9]。这当然不意味着机器已经拥有与数学家等量齐观的理解力，但它至少说明，“先发现什么值得证明”这一步正在被重新组织，而这恰恰是过去通常被看作最依赖人类直觉的环节。
[46] 把这些案例并列起来看，一个共同点会变得很明显：AI for Science 真正改变的，不只是答案出现得更快，而是问题如何被排列、候选如何被筛出、实验如何被调用。也正是在这个意义上，人工智能进入科学发现过程，不应只被理解为工具升级，而更接近一种知识生产范式的结构性变化。
[47] 不过，流程被重组，并不等于理解就会自动增长。AI 越深入科学发现，越有必要继续追问一个老问题：预测成功，到底能不能直接等同于科学理解的增长。这个区分如果不做清楚，很多看似耀眼的成果都可能停留在“有效”而非“被理解”的层面。
[48] 六、AI for Science 的认识论限度
[49] 讨论到这里，认识论上的问题就不能回避了。Krenn 等人特别强调，科学理解并不只取决于结果是否命中，还取决于研究者能否说明其成立条件、适用边界以及它与既有理论之间的关系[11]。顺着这一点往下看，AI for Science 目前最突出的长处，确实是搜索能力和关联能力的大幅提高，但这并不意味着机制解释已经同步成熟。
[50] 对基础研究来说，这个区分尤其不能被轻轻带过。模型很擅长从复杂数据里抓住相关结构，可真正的科学解释往往还要继续回答机制、因果和边界条件这些更难的问题。如果共同体过早把高命中率直接换算成高理解力，表面上像是方法进步，实际上却可能压缩理论阐释和反思的空间。
[51] 还有一个容易被忽视的地方，是模型处理的知识来源本身并不透明。Messeri 与 Crockett 之所以有启发性，就在于他们提醒研究者警惕一种“理解幻象”[12]。已有文献、数据库和实验记录在进入模型之前，就已经带着学科共同体长期积累下来的关注焦点、分类方式和研究盲区。当模型输出足够复杂、结果又足够显著时，研究者便很容易误以为自己已经真正把握了对象。问题未必出在模型“没用”，而更可能出在我们过早把有效预测等同于充分认识。
[52] 说到底，AI 眼下最突出的能力，仍然是快速搜索、压缩空间和重组线索，而不是自己给出机制说明。它当然能够帮助研究者更快逼近值得研究的问题，可一旦涉及“为什么成立”，最后仍然离不开理论判断、实验验证和解释工作。若把这两类能力混成一回事，很多所谓突破就容易停在方法成功的层面。
[53] 也正因为如此，治理问题不能被放到技术成熟之后再来补课。如果 AI for Science 已经进入知识生产内部，那么治理本身就是新范式能否成立的条件之一。它不属于外围修饰，而是这套结构能否长期稳定运转的内部要求。
[54] 首先要重新审视的，其实是评价尺度。现在很多研究过于看重最优结果、最高命中率和最漂亮的性能表格，而对解释是否充分、失败是否被报告、结论边界是否被说明、结果能否被复核，重视明显不够。时间一长，科研共同体就很容易被“可发表的漂亮结果”牵着走。
[55] 如果资源分配始终沿着单一性能逻辑展开，最先被挤压的往往不是短期成果，而是机制解释、失败报告和边界条件研究。久而久之，论文叙述、经费配置乃至研究议程都会越来越围绕“能不能出结果”展开，而不是“我们到底理解了什么”。
[56] 因此，在本文看来，治理并不是 AI for Science 之外的附属议题，而是这套新知识生产结构能否稳住自身秩序的内部条件。若对平台逻辑、责任分配和评价机制缺少同步调整，模型能力越强，科研秩序反而越可能被单一性能导向牵着走。
[57] 还需要补充的一点，是公平问题。Gao 与 Wang 的研究提醒我们，AI 的扩散不仅改变了科研产出的数量，也在重新分配科研影响力和先发优势[13]。谁能够稳定获得高质量数据、充足算力和平台接入权限，决定的已经不只是研究效率，还决定着谁更容易进入新的科研范式并参与规则塑造。如果这种结构长期固化，那么 AI for Science 带来的就不只是能力提升，也可能是知识生产不平等的进一步放大。
[58] 结语
[59] 回过头看，AI for Science 的意义显然不能被压缩成一套单纯的提效叙事。更深的变化在于，人工智能正在重新安排对象如何被表征、证据如何被组织、结论又如何被确认。由此被改变的，不只是理论、数据与实验的配合方式，也是科学家在其中承担的角色、责任和判断位置。
[60] 从自然辩证法的立场看，AI for Science 更像是科学认识中介的一次明显扩展。中介一旦扩展，人类确实更容易进入复杂问题空间，也更有可能在更短时间内找到有效候选；但这并不意味着理解本身会自动加深。中介越强，新的黑箱、依赖关系和资源不平等也可能越突出。因此，评价 AI for Science 不能只停在性能数字上，还必须把解释性、可复核性、责任归属和公平性放在一起考虑。
[61] 因此，本文更愿意把 AI for Science 看成一种仍在形成中的科学新条件，而不是已经完全定型的成功范式。它能否从一轮技术热潮真正沉淀为稳定的科学能力，最终取决于三件事能否一起推进：认识论上的反思，方法论上的调整，以及制度层面的治理。把这三者放到同一问题框架里讨论，也正是自然辩证法在今天仍然具有现实意义的原因。
[64] 参考文献
[65] [1] WANG H, FU T, DU Y, et al. Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence[J]. Nature, 2023, 620: 47-60. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06221-2.
[66] [2] KUHN T S. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions[M]. 4th ed. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2012.
[67] [3] JUMPER J, EVANS R, PRITZEL A, et al. Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold[J]. Nature, 2021, 596: 583-589. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2.
[68] [4] STOKES J M, YANG K, SWANSON K, et al. A deep learning approach to antibiotic discovery[J]. Cell, 2020, 180(4): 688-702.e13. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2020.01.021.
[69] [5] MERCHANT A, BATZNER S, SCHOENHOLZ S S, et al. Scaling deep learning for materials discovery[J]. Nature, 2023, 624: 80-85. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06735-9.
[70] [6] SZYMANSKI N J, RENDY B, FEI Y, et al. An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials[J]. Nature, 2023, 624: 86-91. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w.
[71] [7] BURGER B, MAFFETTONE P M, GUSEV V V, et al. A mobile robotic chemist[J]. Nature, 2020, 583: 237-241. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.
[72] [8] DAVIES A, VELICKOVIC P, BUESING L, et al. Advancing mathematics by guiding human intuition with AI[J]. Nature, 2021, 600: 70-74. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04086-x.
[73] [9] ROMERA-PAREDES B, BAREKATAIN M, NOVIKOV A, et al. Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models[J]. Nature, 2024, 625: 468-475. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06924-6.
[74] [10] TSHITOYAN V, DAGDELEN J, WESTON L, et al. Unsupervised word embeddings capture latent knowledge from materials science literature[J]. Nature, 2019, 571: 95-98. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1335-8.
[75] [11] KRENN M, POLLICE R, GUO S Y, et al. On scientific understanding with artificial intelligence[J]. Nature Reviews Physics, 2022, 4: 761-769. DOI: 10.1038/s42254-022-00518-3.
[76] [12] MESSERI L, CROCKETT M J. Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research[J]. Nature, 2024, 627: 49-58. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07146-0.
[77] [13] GAO J, WANG D. Quantifying the use and potential benefits of artificial intelligence in scientific research[J]. Nature Human Behaviour, 2024, 8: 2281-2292. DOI: 10.1038/s41562-024-02020-5.

- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive to emit inline code review findings (or when a user asks you to call out specific lines).
- Emit one directive per finding; emit none when there are no findings.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3), confidence (0-1).
- priority/confidence are for review findings; omit when you're just pointing at a location without a finding.
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2 confidence=0.55}

### Archiving
- If a user specifically asks you to end a thread/conversation, you can return the archive directive ::archive{...} to archive the thread/conversation.
- Example: ::archive{reason="User requested to end conversation"}
</app-context>
