t = {
12: 'When Scientific Discovery Comes to Depend on Models: The Reorganization of Knowledge Production in AI for Science from the Perspective of the Dialectics of Nature',
13: 'Abstract: In recent years, AI for Science has no longer been merely a buzzword in technical publicity, but has become a new variable that is genuinely entering scientific practice. Many discussions first notice the acceleration brought by computing power, models, and automated experimentation. This paper, however, is more concerned with another question: when models, data, and experiments begin to be re-embedded in one another\'s workflows, in what sense is scientific knowledge being produced? Drawing on the analytical framework of the dialectics of nature concerning practice, mediation, and the subject-object relation, this paper discusses the structural impact of AI for Science on the mode of scientific discovery. It argues that the key change lies neither in whether machines will replace scientists nor in whether data will overwhelm theory, but in the reordering of the original division of labor among theory, data, and experiment. Data enter the starting point of research earlier, models become more deeply involved in object representation and candidate generation, and experiments increasingly undertake the tasks of verification, calibration, and correction. Correspondingly, the role of scientists has not disappeared; rather, it has become more concentrated in problem formulation, result interpretation, and responsible judgment. If evaluation continues to revolve mainly around predictive accuracy and screening efficiency, problems such as insufficient explanation, platform black boxes, diluted responsibility, and the reconcentration of research resources will easily be obscured. On this basis, this paper proposes that AI for Science should be understood as a structural reorganization of the production of scientific knowledge, and that explanatory power, reproducibility, and institutional legitimacy should serve as more appropriate standards of evaluation.',
14: 'Keywords: AI for Science; dialectics of nature; production of scientific knowledge; scientific intelligence; human-AI collaboration; research governance',
16: 'Introduction',
17: 'In recent years, artificial intelligence has entered basic scientific research faster than many people expected. AlphaFold has changed the starting point of protein structure research; materials discovery increasingly relies on models to compress the search space in advance; and mathematical research has also begun to feel the inspiration brought by large models and program search [3][5][9]. Taken together, these developments make one fact difficult to avoid: artificial intelligence is no longer merely auxiliary computing power at the periphery of research. It is gradually entering the process of discovery itself.',
18: 'Around this transformation, recent discussions in leading journals have already formed several interrelated lines of inquiry. Wang et al. emphasize that the significance of AI for Science lies in the way models, data, and automated experimentation are jointly reshaping the infrastructure of scientific discovery [1]. Krenn et al. remind us that more accurate prediction does not necessarily mean deeper understanding [11]. Messeri and Crockett further point out that if researchers too quickly treat model outputs as evidence that they have already understood a phenomenon, they may fall into an illusion in which explanation remains poor although the method appears successful [12]. Taken together, these studies suggest that what deserves examination is no longer efficiency alone, but whether the cognitive structure inside scientific research has been rewritten.',
19: 'A clear limitation of existing discussion is that much analysis remains at the level of application: AI is either regarded as a stronger research tool or imagined directly as a substitute subject. This paper is more concerned with the intermediate layer, namely how the relations among theory, data, experiment, and scientists\' judgment change after models enter the discovery process. Placing this question back within the perspective of the dialectics of nature, we see not simply technological upgrading, but the reorganization of relations among subject, object, and mediation. The epistemological meaning and governance consequences of this reorganization are precisely what this paper seeks to discuss.',
20: 'I. Framing the Problem: AI for Science Should Not Be Reduced to a Tool of Efficiency',
21: 'It is certainly reasonable to say that AI for Science makes research faster, but this judgment is not sufficient. Protein structure prediction, drug discovery, and materials design all show that models have greatly compressed the time required for high-dimensional search and improved the efficiency of candidate ranking [3][4][5]. Yet scientific research is not simply a race for speed. However quickly results arrive, they can hardly become substantial knowledge unless they enter the chain of explanation, verification, and recognition by the scientific community. For this reason, AI for Science is better understood as a knowledge condition that may change the order of research.',
22: 'This is exactly where the problem lies. Scientific research does not end when an optimal solution is calculated. Researchers must still explain why a result holds, where its limits of applicability lie, and how it connects with existing theory. In other words, scientific discovery is both a technical process and a knowledge process; it involves performance indicators as well as mechanistic explanation; it depends on experiment and computation, while also being constrained by the collective judgment of the community concerning what can count as evidence. If this layer is removed and only efficiency remains, the most essential part of scientific activity becomes invisible.',
23: 'Therefore, what truly deserves discussion is not efficiency improvement itself, but whether the chain of knowledge production has been rewritten. In the past, although theory, data, and experiment were not always arranged in a strictly linear sequence, their division of labor was generally stable: theory proposed explanatory frameworks and hypotheses, experiment undertook testing, and data usually entered analysis as evidential results. This arrangement is now loosening. Data enter object representation and model training earlier; models begin to participate in candidate generation and the compression of research paths; and experiments increasingly perform the functions of feedback, calibration, and correction. What AI for Science touches is precisely this internal working order of scientific discovery.',
24: 'If this change is placed back within the perspective of the dialectics of nature, the issue cannot be understood merely as whether the technology is useful. A more important question is how humans and objects establish relations when models become a prior link through which researchers approach objects, and within what kind of chain of mediation knowledge is organized. Efficiency improvement is certainly important, but if AI for Science is treated only as an accelerator of research, its deeper influence on cognitive pathways and modes of evidential organization will easily be overlooked.',
25: 'II. AI as a Cognitive Mediator and the Reorganization of the Subject-Object Relation',
26: 'The dialectics of nature has long reminded us that scientific cognition is not a direct face-to-face encounter between subject and object, but always unfolds through a series of mediations. Experimental apparatuses, mathematical models, measurement techniques, symbolic systems, and collaborative networks all play a role. In many cases, the truly important leap in the history of science has not been that the object suddenly revealed itself, but that human beings found a new mediator and thereby obtained a new path for approaching the object.',
27: 'Viewed in this context, AI differs from ordinary computational tools not only because it calculates faster, but because it intervenes simultaneously in representation, screening, generation, and feedback. Once an object is translated into a computable representation, the model no longer merely executes commands passively. It begins to participate in judging what deserves attention, what should be prioritized for experiment, and which anomalies should be pursued further. In this sense, AI is no longer merely one component in a workflow; to a certain extent, it rewrites the workflow of discovery itself.',
28: 'More precisely, what is rewritten is not only the workflow, but also the way researchers approach their objects. In traditional experimental science, subjects mainly face objects through observation, measurement, and manipulation. In AI for Science, however, objects often have to be processed first into sequences, graph structures, crystal representations, or reaction networks before they enter model space for comparison, ranking, and prediction. Thus an additional layer of mediation emerges between subject and object, composed of datasets, representation schemes, loss functions, search strategies, and platform rules. Objects no longer appear only in the form of natural entities; they also enter research as computable representations. Researchers\' work correspondingly shifts more toward data governance, model scrutiny, and responsibility for explanation.',
29: 'Of course, an increase in mediation brings not only expanded capacity but also new constraints. Models do enable researchers to enter high-dimensional problem spaces that were previously difficult to handle, but through the boundaries of training data, the settings of objective functions, and the preferences embedded in platform rules, they can also redistribute researchers\' attention. In other words, AI makes it easier for subjects to grasp objects, while it may quietly delimit the very ways in which subjects are able to grasp them. Because these two sides coexist, AI for Science cannot simply be described as a tool upgrade; it should be understood as a mediating condition that changes cognitive pathways.',
30: 'III. The Reorganization of Relations among Theory, Data, and Experiment',
31: 'This transformation becomes clearer when the issue is placed within the relations among theory, data, and experiment. Borrowing Kuhn\'s discussion of paradigm change to understand the present situation [2], what we see is not a partial acceleration of research along its original track, but a structural adjustment in the organization of research itself. Traditional scientific practice also involved repeated back-and-forth movement, but for a long time the basic pattern remained relatively stable: theory proposed hypotheses, experiment provided tests, and data served as evidential results. What has truly changed today is the sequence, weighting, and coupling of these three elements.',
32: 'The first change concerns the position of data. In the past, data appeared more often in the later stages of research as result material. Now data increasingly function as a precondition for research to begin. The reason models can predict protein conformations, generate materials candidates, or capture potential reaction pathways is first that large amounts of existing data have already been organized into computable forms. In particular, the widespread use of literature embeddings and database learning means that existing knowledge is no longer merely text and figures for researchers to read; it also becomes part of the training samples and representation space, thereby determining in advance what the model is able to see [10].',
33: 'At the same time, the model is no longer only an auxiliary component that calculates faster. It is more like an intermediate layer placed between data and experiment: on one end, it extracts features from existing data and compresses the search space; on the other, it sends candidate rankings, property predictions, and parameter suggestions back to the experimental stage. Precisely because the model is embedded between these two directions, the research process increasingly ceases to resemble a linear sequence of several steps and instead becomes a cycle of prediction, verification, and retraining.',
34: 'The position of experiment is also shifting as a result. The enhancement of model capability has not made experiment lose its value. On the contrary, the responsibilities of experiment have become more focused. More and more studies no longer begin with broad blind trial and error; instead, models first compress the candidate space, and limited experimental resources are then directed toward key variables and anomalous results. In this way, experiment is not merely the final confirmation of conclusions, but a feedback mechanism that continuously participates in model revision, result calibration, and adjustment of research direction.',
35: 'What must not be ignored here, however, is theory. In reality, theory has not been submerged by data; rather, it has changed position. On the one hand, theory continues to provide boundaries for object representation, variable selection, target setting, and result evaluation, preventing models from searching blindly in the absence of disciplinary constraints. On the other hand, anomalous candidates, unexpected correlations, and failed results produced by models can in turn force theory to revise its existing explanations. Thus theory, data, and experiment no longer appear as three relatively segmented steps, but as a circuit of continuous return and mutual correction. Rather than saying that data replace theory or models replace experiment, it is more accurate to say that a new collaborative structure has formed among the three.',
36: 'IV. The Migration and Reconstruction of Scientists\' Subjectivity',
37: 'As models and automated platforms become more deeply embedded in research workflows, people often worry that scientists will be marginalized in the process of discovery. At least at the present stage, the issue is not whether the scientific subject will simply be replaced, but that the focus of its work has already shifted. In the past, a great deal of time was spent on candidate search, repeated trial and error, manual screening, and technical adjustment. Today, part of these processes is being taken over by models and platforms. Yet whether the problem has been accurately formulated, whether anomalous results deserve further pursuit, whether a mechanistic explanation is valid, and how far a conclusion should be extended all depend even more on researchers\' judgment.',
38: 'However, a shift in the focus of work does not automatically mean an enhancement of subjectivity. If researchers simply follow the rankings, recommendations, and default paths provided by systems, scientific practice may gradually slide from humans using tools toward humans obeying platform logic. This weakening does not appear as the absence of scientists, but as the pre-shaping of judgments that should have been made by humans within platform rules. What truly needs vigilance is not whether humans remain in the loop, but whether the authority over key judgments remains firmly in the hands of researchers themselves.',
39: 'Therefore, when discussing scientific subjectivity under the condition of AI, the key question is not whether researchers once again master every technical detail, but whether they can maintain stable judgment and critical capacity toward the entire mediating system. Whether training data contain systematic biases, whether an objective function truly corresponds to the research question, whether statistical significance is mistaken for mechanistic importance, whether anomalous results have been automatically filtered out, and how strong a conclusion should be stated are all matters that cannot be handed over to platform defaults. In other words, scientists have not become lighter because of the introduction of AI; rather, the content of subjectivity has moved from the operational level toward the levels of judgment and responsibility.',
40: 'V. Paradigm Changes in Representative Cases',
41: 'If the above discussion remains only at the conceptual level, it may seem somewhat abstract. The issue becomes clearer if we begin with several of the most representative papers published in leading journals in recent years. The following discussion mainly selects AlphaFold\'s transformation of the starting point of structural biology [3], GNoME\'s reorganization of the materials search space [5], the entry of autonomous laboratories into inorganic materials synthesis [6], and the participation of large language models in mathematical discovery [9], in order to show concretely how AI changes the starting point of research, the organization of evidence, and the structure of collaboration.',
42: 'Take AlphaFold as an example. The importance of Jumper et al.\'s work lies not only in pushing the accuracy of protein structure prediction to a new level, but also in quietly rewriting the starting point of structural biology [3]. In the past, many studies often had to spend considerable time obtaining structural clues before subsequent functional analysis and mechanistic explanation could unfold. AlphaFold, however, provides sufficiently strong prior structural information, allowing many studies to form preliminary hypotheses from model predictions first and then concentrate experimental resources on functional verification, mechanistic analysis, and the examination of boundary conditions. The change in the starting point of research itself shows that the model has already entered the front end of the knowledge production chain.',
43: 'Changes in materials discovery are also typical. Merchant et al.\'s study of GNoME shows that the value of deep learning models lies not merely in finding more candidate crystals, but more importantly in compressing in advance a vast search space that could hardly be exhaustively explored directly [5]. Once this front-end work is completed by models, the directionality of subsequent experiments is significantly strengthened. In other words, models no longer simply make existing steps faster; at the front end, they participate in judging which objects are worth trying first.',
44: 'The case of autonomous laboratories makes this platform tendency even more apparent. Szymanski et al. show that several links can already be connected into a relatively continuous closed loop: models propose candidates, databases accumulate historical results, experimental devices carry out synthesis, and feedback systems promptly return new results to the model [6]. If Burger et al.\'s work on a mobile robotic chemist is also taken into account, it becomes even clearer that such systems are not single-point automation, but are evolving toward platformized experimental organization [7]. Once this structure truly operates, scientific activity can hardly still be described as a simple sequence of theory, experiment, and analysis. It more closely resembles a continuous loop maintained by multiple technical mediators.',
45: 'The mathematical case provides another important perspective. Studies by Romera-Paredes et al. and Davies et al. both show that large language models and program search can already participate in pattern recognition, conjecture generation, and even the discovery of heuristic paths toward proof in mathematical problems [8][9]. This certainly does not mean that machines have an understanding equivalent to that of mathematicians. But it at least shows that the step of first discovering what is worth proving is being reorganized, and this step was traditionally regarded as one of the parts most dependent on human intuition.',
46: 'When these cases are placed side by side, one common feature becomes obvious: what AI for Science truly changes is not only that answers appear faster, but how problems are arranged, how candidates are screened, and how experiments are mobilized. It is in this sense that the entry of artificial intelligence into the process of scientific discovery should not be understood merely as a tool upgrade, but as a structural transformation of the paradigm of knowledge production.',
47: 'Nevertheless, the reorganization of workflow does not mean that understanding will automatically grow. The deeper AI enters scientific discovery, the more necessary it becomes to return to an old question: can predictive success be directly equated with the growth of scientific understanding? If this distinction is not made clearly, many apparently impressive achievements may remain at the level of being effective rather than understood.',
48: 'VI. The Epistemological Limits of AI for Science',
49: 'At this point, epistemological questions can no longer be avoided. Krenn et al. particularly emphasize that scientific understanding does not depend only on whether a result is correct; it also depends on whether researchers can explain the conditions under which it holds, the boundaries of its applicability, and its relation to existing theory [11]. Following this point, the most prominent strengths of AI for Science at present are indeed greatly improved search capacity and correlation-detection capacity, but this does not mean that mechanistic explanation has matured at the same pace.',
50: 'For basic research, this distinction must not be passed over lightly. Models are good at capturing correlated structures in complex data, but genuine scientific explanation must continue to answer more difficult questions about mechanisms, causality, and boundary conditions. If the community too quickly converts high hit rates directly into high levels of understanding, the surface appearance may be methodological progress, while in fact the space for theoretical interpretation and reflection may be compressed.',
51: 'Another easily neglected issue is that the sources of knowledge processed by models are not themselves transparent. The insight of Messeri and Crockett lies in their warning against an illusion of understanding [12]. Before existing literature, databases, and experimental records enter models, they already carry the focal points, classification schemes, and research blind spots accumulated by the disciplinary community over time. When model outputs are sufficiently complex and results sufficiently significant, researchers may easily assume that they have truly grasped the object. The problem may not be that the model is useless, but that we too quickly equate effective prediction with adequate knowledge.',
52: 'Ultimately, the most prominent abilities of AI at present remain rapid search, compression of problem spaces, and recombination of clues, rather than the independent provision of mechanistic explanation. AI can of course help researchers approach worthwhile questions more quickly. Yet once the question becomes why something holds, theoretical judgment, experimental verification, and explanatory work remain indispensable. If these two kinds of ability are confused, many so-called breakthroughs may stop at the level of methodological success.',
53: 'For this reason, governance cannot be postponed until after the technology has matured. If AI for Science has already entered the interior of knowledge production, then governance itself is one of the conditions under which the new paradigm can be established. It is not an external embellishment, but an internal requirement for whether this structure can operate stably over the long term.',
54: 'The first issue that needs to be reexamined is the scale of evaluation. At present, many studies attach too much importance to optimal results, the highest hit rates, and the most attractive performance tables, while paying obviously insufficient attention to whether explanations are adequate, whether failures are reported, whether the boundaries of conclusions are stated, and whether results can be reproduced. Over time, the scientific community can easily be led by publishable and visually impressive results.',
55: 'If the allocation of resources always follows a single performance logic, what is first squeezed out is often not short-term output, but mechanistic explanation, failure reporting, and research on boundary conditions. In the long run, paper narratives, funding allocation, and even research agendas will increasingly revolve around whether results can be produced rather than what we have actually understood.',
56: 'Therefore, in the view of this paper, governance is not an auxiliary issue outside AI for Science, but an internal condition for whether this new structure of knowledge production can stabilize its own order. If platform logic, responsibility allocation, and evaluation mechanisms are not adjusted at the same time, the stronger model capabilities become, the more likely the order of research is to be driven by a single performance orientation.',
57: 'One further point concerns fairness. Gao and Wang remind us that the diffusion of AI is changing not only the quantity of research output, but also the distribution of scientific influence and first-mover advantages [13]. Who can consistently obtain high-quality data, sufficient computing power, and access to platforms determines not only research efficiency, but also who is more likely to enter the new research paradigm and participate in shaping its rules. If this structure becomes entrenched over the long term, AI for Science may bring not only enhanced capacity, but also a further amplification of inequality in knowledge production.',
58: 'Conclusion',
59: 'Looking back, the significance of AI for Science clearly cannot be compressed into a simple narrative of efficiency improvement. The deeper change lies in the fact that artificial intelligence is rearranging how objects are represented, how evidence is organized, and how conclusions are confirmed. What is changed as a result is not only the coordination among theory, data, and experiment, but also the role, responsibility, and position of judgment assumed by scientists within this process.',
60: 'From the standpoint of the dialectics of nature, AI for Science is more like a significant expansion of the mediators of scientific cognition. Once mediation expands, human beings can indeed enter complex problem spaces more easily and may find effective candidates in a shorter time. But this does not mean that understanding itself will automatically deepen. The stronger the mediator becomes, the more prominent new black boxes, dependencies, and inequalities of resources may become. Therefore, the evaluation of AI for Science cannot stop at performance figures; it must also consider explainability, reproducibility, responsibility attribution, and fairness together.',
61: 'Therefore, this paper is more inclined to regard AI for Science as a new scientific condition still in formation, rather than as a fully established successful paradigm. Whether it can truly settle from a wave of technological enthusiasm into a stable scientific capability ultimately depends on whether three tasks can be advanced together: epistemological reflection, methodological adjustment, and institutional governance. Discussing these three within the same problem framework is precisely why the dialectics of nature still has practical significance today.',
64: 'References',
65: '[1] WANG H, FU T, DU Y, et al. Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence[J]. Nature, 2023, 620: 47-60. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06221-2.',
66: '[2] KUHN T S. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions[M]. 4th ed. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2012.',
